items.title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.original_title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.summary: Iran has warned that merchant ships switching off their identification and tracking equipment during what it deems unauthorised passages through the Strait of Hormuz will be treated as hostile, raising the stakes for vessels navigating one of the world’s most dangerous stretches of water. The warning comes as fresh details emerge of a wave of attacks on Sunday that extended beyond tankers to containerships. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued four retrospective alerts on Monday covering three tankers and a containership struck on October 11, bringing the day’s reported total to six. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), meanwhile, claimed to have attacked a VLCC attempting to transit without permission, releasing footage purportedly showing the fire-damaged, 298,800 dwt Al Maqam , owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. It remains unclear whether the purported strike was among those reported by UKMTO or represents another incident. Two Indian seafarers remain missing after Sunday’s drone strike on the Nicaragua-flagged Petro Dolphin off Sohar, Oman. Nine crewmembers were rescued. The latest violence follows Saturday’s American airstrike against the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman, with Washington accusing the vessel of attempting to breach its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

items.title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.original_title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.summary: France has taken its crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet into the Indian Ocean, boarding a former Sovcomflot aframax more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion. French marines descended by helicopter onto the 110,119 dwt DF Peak on Monday after authorities questioned the validity of its claimed Benin registration. President Emmanuel Macron said the vessel was suspected of sailing under a false flag and involvement in illicit fuel transportation. “France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world,” Macron declared. The French military said the boarding was conducted under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which permits inspections of vessels suspected of lacking valid nationality. Built in 2006, the tanker previously traded as NS Captain for Russian state-controlled Sovcomflot before becoming Kaliningrad in 2024 and subsequently DF Peak. The vessel has been under EU sanctions since June 2024 and is also blacklisted by Washington and London. Ukrainian intelligence links the ship to Russian crude exports. The operation follows several French interventions against Russia-linked tankers in European waters, including the interception of the Deliver off Sicily in June.

items.title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.original_title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.summary: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has joined forces with classification society ABS to accelerate the development of commercial nuclear-powered shipping and floating power plants. The agreement with DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy covers feasibility studies for floating reactors, dedicated nuclear shipping corridors and the ports, shipyards and industrial infrastructure required to build and support nuclear-powered vessels. ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group, providing technical, regulatory and economic expertise, while coordinating related work through the US Maritime Administration’s Center for Maritime Innovation. “Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS chairman and CEO John McDonald. In 2022, DOE contracted ABS to examine barriers to commercial nuclear propulsion, while the class society subsequently published the industry’s first comprehensive rules for floating nuclear power plants. As Splash reported in July, ABS approved in principle a South Korean 15,000 teu containership concept incorporating a molten salt reactor, following earlier approvals for floating nuclear power modules developed by HD Hyundai. Last month, ABS backed a study examining the economics of a 174,000 cu m nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The vessel would cost approximately 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional LNG carrier, although researchers projected lower lifetime costs under certain carbon-pricing scenarios.

items.title: TGS expands frontier basin data coverage offshore Brazil
items.original_title: TGS expands frontier basin data coverage offshore Brazil
items.summary: Oslo-listed seismic specialist TGS, in joint venture with SLB, has announced the Pelotas Sul Phase 2 multi-client 3D survey offshore southern Brazil. The survey will cover about 11,200 sq km, and a Ramform Titan-class vessel is scheduled to begin data acquisition in October 2026, with completion in the second or third quarter of 2027. Building on Pelotas Sul Phase 1, acquired earlier this year, the new survey will further expand TGS’ high-quality 3D seismic coverage in a frontier basin that continues to attract industry interest. Geological analogues along the conjugate margin support the Pelotas Basin, and discoveries in Namibia de-risk it. The basin offers a broad range of underexplored play concepts, including turbidite systems, deep-water channels, and stratigraphic and structural traps. Pelotas Sul Phase 2 includes a balanced mix of held and open acreage. This provides data coverage relevant to companies evaluating existing acreage, while also creating opportunities linked to future licensing rounds and potential farm-in activity. “The project will provide additional high-quality subsurface insight across both held and open acreage, supporting our customers as they evaluate existing positions and future exploration opportunities in the southern Pelotas Basin,” said Kristian Johansen, CEO of TGS.

items.title: Soaring Tanker Rates Leave Americas Awash in Crude Oil
items.original_title: Soaring Tanker Rates Leave Americas Awash in Crude Oil
items.summary: HOUSTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) – Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and US refiners have been running close to their limits. The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above $100 a barrel. Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many US, and some European refineries are typically configured to process. Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity. Many US refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock.

items.title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.original_title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.summary: Spot rates have become more volatile, relative to the wider box shipping market, since the pandemic, with overall prices increasingly diverging from signals provided by the spot market. In its latest analysis, Sea-Intelligence, compared spot rate movements on the Asia-Europe and transpacific trades with broader market developments, using World Container Index (WCI) and Container Trade Statistics (CTS) data. The consultant compared monthly average WCI rates for Shanghai-Rotterdam and Shanghai-Genoa with CTS data for Asia-Europe. Sea-Intelligence used this relationship to forecast the overall market rate index from spot rate movements, and then compared its predictions with the actual CTS figures. Before the pandemic disruptions, Sea-Intelligence found, the difference between forecast and actual market rates fluctuated relatively little, suggesting spot rates provided a reasonably reliable indication of wider market developments. However, deviations became substantially larger from 2020, which the analyst said reflected a greater disconnect between spot rate movements and the market as a whole – also evident when fluctuations were measured relative to overall rate levels, meaning it could not simply be attributed to higher freight rates. Sea-Intelligence also identified a gradual upward trend in the difference between forecast and actual rates on Asia-Europe, indicating that the overall market increasingly recorded higher rates than would have been predicted from spot prices alone.

items.title: Why are EU gas prices not higher already?
items.original_title: Why are EU gas prices not higher already?
items.summary: European natural gas prices have remained relatively contained despite major disruptions to Middle Eastern liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports, as additional supply and weaker demand have cushioned the impact, according to UBS analysts. In an October 5 report, UBS said higher LNG production outside the Middle East and reduced consumption across Europe and Asia had helped offset supply losses caused by the Iran war. Middle Eastern LNG supply declined by approximately 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) between March and September, while additional production elsewhere contributed nearly 40 bcm, including 17 bcm from the United States. European gas storage remains roughly 15% below seasonal averages, with inventories expected to enter winter at 74% capacity and decline to approximately 25% by spring. UBS consequently raised its fourth-quarter Dutch TTF gas price forecast to €75 per megawatt-hour from €62 previously. Its 2027 forecast increased to €45 from €40, reflecting expectations of a slower recovery in Qatari LNG exports and continued European efforts to phase out Russian gas. Under a prolonged disruption scenario accompanied by colder weather, UBS sees fourth-quarter TTF prices averaging €90/MWh, with potential peaks near €120/MWh. A faster recovery in Qatari shipments and milder temperatures could instead bring fourth-quarter prices towards €50/MWh.

items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd suspends bookings to three Philippine ports as container crisis deepens
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has suspended new bookings to Manila, Batangas and Subic Bay until the end of December, as worsening congestion and a chronic shortage of empty-container storage capacity disrupt Philippine supply chains. The German carrier stopped accepting bookings to the three gateways from all origins and across every trade lane on September 29, citing severe constraints on container returns. Existing bookings may also face cancellation or revised arrangements. The crisis centres on the Philippines’ longstanding trade imbalance, with significantly more laden containers arriving than departing, leaving carriers struggling to find space for empty boxes. Philippine Ports Authority general manager Jay Santiago has urged foreign shipping lines to establish additional empty-container depots, describing this as the quickest solution to the worsening logistics bottleneck. Mary Zapata, president of the Confederation of Truckers Associations of the Philippines, told local newspaper Daily Tribune that some operators have waited as long as 40 days to return empty boxes. The problems triggered industrial action earlier this month, prompting the Philippine Bureau of Customs to acknowledge the severe pressure on truckers, customs brokers, importers and exporters. Subic Bay waiting times, however, remain below 12 hours, while Batangas operations are described as normal.

items.title: Pollution Risk from Overboard Pipes Routed Through Fuel Oil Tanks
items.original_title: Pollution Risk from Overboard Pipes Routed Through Fuel Oil Tanks
items.summary: There have been two more pollution incidents arising from a similar arrangement. In both cases, an Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment (ODME) overboard discharge pipe was routed through a bunker fuel tank before terminating at the ship’s side. Why These Arrangements Warrant Attention An overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank can create a single-point failure with potentially significant pollution consequences. If a defect develops in a section of pipe located between the isolation overboard valve and the vessel’s shell, fuel oil may enter the pipe downstream of the closed valve and continue flowing directly overboard. Recommended Actions The West of England strongly recommends that Members and ship managers review the overboard piping arrangements across their fleets, giving particular attention to any overboard pipe that passes through a bunker or cargo oil tank and is capable of creating a direct route between a tank containing oil and the sea following loss of pipe integrity. Members may wish to consider the following: Identify Vulnerable Arrangements Review piping diagrams, tank plans, construction drawings and onboard arrangements to identify any overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank. Review Maintenance and Inspection Programmes Planned maintenance systems should identify and specifically address concealed or difficult-to-access overboard pipework routed through oil tanks.

The price of that surplus now shapes how shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers weigh their options, yet much of the industry still has to estimate what pooling really costs. Rystad Energy and OceanScore are working together to close that gap. Under a new data agreement, Rystad Energy will integrate two sets of OceanScore data. The first is offer data from the OceanScore FuelEU Marketplace, where surplus providers post offers to companies holding compliance deficits. The second is the OceanScore Pool Price Index (OPX), a volume-weighted benchmark for FuelEU pooling prices. The data will feed into Rystad Energy’s Clean Shipping Solution, which tracks the maritime energy transition across fleet development, ports and bunkering, fuel costs, and fuel supply and demand. When decisions across the value chain rest on observed market data, the transition can move faster and with fewer costly surprises. Source: Rystad Energy

items.title: Back to Suez – Why the rush?
items.original_title: Back to Suez – Why the rush?
items.summary: This is an extract from the Container Forecaster Issue 3 2026, released 30 September. The apparent eagerness of container lines to return to the Suez Canal is difficult to explain if the calculation is reduced to a simple voyage-cost comparison between Suez and the Cape. Drewry’s slot cost comparison shows only a marginal economic benefit to using Suez (see Table 1) with a saving of approximately $1 million per round-voyage, or $43 per slot, when comparing two services deploying ships of 24,000 teu that use either Suez or the Cape in both directions. If we assume a valuation of $225 million for the same example 24,000 teu containership going through Suez from Asia to Europe, a one-way war-risk premium of 0.3% of the hull value would heap an extra $1.35m for a round-voyage with two trips through the Joint War Committee listed area. The more convincing explanation for why carriers are so keen to return to Suez is that they are not really making a binary Suez versus Cape voyage decision based on economics alone. As such, we have adjusted our base case assumptions to a phase back of Suez transits starting July/August of 2026, reaching 80% of pre-diversion level by February 2027.

items.title: High stake fuel decisions
items.original_title: High stake fuel decisions
items.summary: That is the challenge at the heart of DNV’s latest white paper on methanol in shipping, which finds that many of the ship-related barriers surrounding methanol have fallen substantially since 2020. The bigger uncertainties now lie in fuel price and availability, regulation and, ultimately, whether owners can formulate strategies robust enough to withstand a changing decarbonisation landscape. Methanol has moved rapidly towards the mainstream. “The analysis should assess a ship or a fleet under a range of varying fuel and CO2 prices, covering all GHG regulations and associated GHG trajectories, to provide a clearer picture of the robustness of each fuel strategy,” DNV says. The strongest candidates then progress to a technical assessment examining what those fuel strategies mean for the actual ship. That covers storage capacity, bunkering frequency and operations, tank designs and possible locations, fuel preparation and supply, energy converters and changes to the vessel’s general arrangement. For owners unwilling to commit immediately to a single alternative fuel, the report also highlights Fuel Ready approaches, under which newbuildings can incorporate preparations for later conversion, including consideration of trim, stability and structural modifications. The fuel remains liquid at ambient temperature and pressure, bunkering infrastructure is comparatively close to conventional bunker arrangements and the technology is relatively mature.

items.title: Russian tanker operators lift crude exports to highest level since G7 price cap
items.original_title: Russian tanker operators lift crude exports to highest level since G7 price cap
items.summary: Russia increased crude exports in September by relying more heavily on non-G7 tankers, particularly those operated by domestic companies, whose shipments reached their highest level since Western nations imposed a price cap. Tankers flagged, owned and operated by companies not based in G7 countries and their allies, and not insured by Western protection and indemnity clubs, lifted nearly 2.89 million barrels/day in September, compared with 2.7 million b/d in August, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data. The increase came as overall Russian seaborne exports rose to 4.09 million b/d from 3.82 million b/d in the same period. While the overall share of Russian crude exports on non-G7 tankers, mainly from the shadow flee established to bypass Western sanctions, showed little change month on month, Russian tanker operators were shouldering more responsibilities for their home country’s overseas sales. Continuing the upward trajectory seen in recent months, shipments rose from 18.6 million barrels in August to 20.6 million barrels in September — the highest since the G7 and EU began banning maritime service firms from participating in Russian crude exports unless the barrels were sold below a certain threshold in December 2022.

items.summary: Maersk's methanol-fueled container vessel Laura Maersk arrives for an official naming ceremony in Copenhagen, Denmark, September 13, 2023. The report, Ethanol as a Marine Fuel: Exploring Its Usability, published Thursday, examines whether ethanol can be used in existing marine engines and what modifications would be needed to make it commercially viable. Maersk has been testing ethanol aboard its methanol-fueled container vessel Laura Maersk since 2025, initially using a 10% ethanol blend before moving to higher concentrations. Despite those limitations, the study found that converting some existing vessels to operate on ethanol blends could make economic sense. For example, researchers found that a large container ship consuming approximately 25,000 tonnes of fuel annually could economically operate on a 30% ethanol blend across a wider range of fuel carbon intensities. The report also stops short of determining how much ethanol could realistically contribute to shipping’s overall decarbonization.

items.title: Is FOMO driving sentiment in the containership charter market?
items.original_title: Is FOMO driving sentiment in the containership charter market?
items.summary: The containership timecharter (T/C) market has taken another lurch upwards in recent months, with numerous participants describing a renewed scramble by liner operators – especially the largest European players – to secure any available tonnage. Most market benchmarks have participated in the recent strengthening, with the assessed one-year T/C rate for MSI’s 1,700 teu Grd (geared) Non-Eco benchmark rising from $28,800 a day in June to $34,100/day in September, and our 6,500 teu Gls [gearless] Non-Eco benchmark increasing from $68,400/day to $78,300/day over the same period. As noted in MSI’s Containerships Q3 26 report, the market cooled a little in the second half of September, compared with the height of the northern hemisphere’s summer, but this remains a market in which non-operating owners (NOOs) are firmly in the driving seat, and charterers are still willing to fix vessels in the liquid market segments for two-to-three years at healthy rates, and often for forward delivery dates. The lack of charter market-sized vessels available to hire, in both the near- and medium-term, means an upward movement in rates is the unsurprising outcome of a renewed fixing drive by the major liners.

items.title: BIMCO moves to break ship retrofit cost deadlock
items.original_title: BIMCO moves to break ship retrofit cost deadlock
items.summary: Shipping association BIMCO has adopted a new contractual framework designed to settle one of the industry’s longstanding commercial disputes: who pays for energy-saving upgrades when the charterer receives much of the financial benefit. The Copenhagen-based organisation announced that its Documentary Committee had approved the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026, giving shipowners and charterers a standard framework for negotiating retrofit projects during existing time charters. The addendum covers how the two parties share installation costs, time implications and the financial gains generated by lower fuel consumption. Rather than setting fixed percentages, it allows the parties to negotiate arrangements for individual projects. BIMCO said the addendum is technology-neutral and can accommodate different energy-saving systems, as well as the financial implications of existing and future environmental regulations. In June, BIMCO said development had reached its final stages, following consultation with industry participants and its Documentary Committee. The drafting process included representatives from Stena Rederi and Cargill Ocean Transportation. The new agreement is intended to provide a common contractual basis for retrofit projects that have previously required individually negotiated commercial arrangements. BIMCO said the addendum would be made available through its SmartCon contract platform, together with explanatory guidance.

items.summary: Lloyd’s List Intelligence (LLI) has launched Satellite Confirmed Spoofing, a new capability within its proprietary maritime intelligence platform, Seasearcher. This new functionality combines AIS spoofing detection with automatic satellite imagery validation, helping compliance, risk and intelligence teams identify deceptive vessel behaviour with greater confidence. The launch reflects growing demand for defensible intelligence, helping maritime organisations prioritise investigations, strengthen compliance processes, and make decisions based on independently validated evidence. Vessels seeking to evade scrutiny are broadcasting false positions that look entirely legitimate,” said Arne Staal, Chief Research Officer at Lloyd’s List Intelligence. “We’ve detected this behaviour for some time, but detection models are by nature probabilistic. We can now take our users from flagging probable spoofing events, to corroborating the event with satellite imagery. For compliance teams, insurers, and regulators, this marks a shift from inference to independent evidence, so they can decisively act on what the imagery shows rather than what a vessel chose to report.” Satellite Confirmed Spoofing is designed to support that mission by helping customers move from an inferred risk signal to a validated event. By combining maritime expertise, advanced analytics and satellite technology, we are making it easier for organisations to identify deceptive shipping practices and understand the evidence behind them. Source: Lloyd’s List Intelligence

items.summary: US liquefied natural gas projects face a competitiveness challenge as domestic natural gas prices continue to rise, according to Fulcrum LNG CEO Jesus Bronchalo. Bronchalo made the remarks Tuesday during a panel discussion at Rice University’s Baker Institute. He said natural gas prices are expected to increase further in the US, which is already among the most expensive locations globally for LNG production. “Henry Hub is going to get to the point where it becomes too expensive or you are not going to be too competitive,” Bronchalo said, referring to the US gas price benchmark. Joshua Lubarsky, president of maritime firm Seapath Group, noted at the same conference that while the US ranks among the world’s highest-cost LNG producers, its gas price dynamics provide stability that appeals to buyers. The financing structure for US LNG projects is shifting, with growing reliance on private equity supported by government-backed sovereign wealth funds, said Julie Mayo, general counsel at Sempra Infrastructure. Mayo pointed to Sempra’s use of private equity funds for expansion as an example of the new financing approach for US LNG projects, moving away from traditional external loans. items.summary: Norwegian shipping investment company Hunter Group’s dispute with an unnamed long-term VLCC charter counterparty has deepened further, with unpaid hire now approaching $68m after another substantial shortfall in September. The Oslo-listed company disclosed on Friday that its counterparty paid approximately $12.75m less than the amount due for September, marking the seventh consecutive month of reduced payments. The latest shortfall takes the total disputed balance to approximately $67.79m, excluding accrued interest, compared with $55.04m a month earlier. Hunter recorded net time charter earnings of approximately $60.88m for September, more than the $31.69m booked in August, although the company said $12.75m of the latest earnings remains outstanding. The counterparty continues to contest its contractual obligation to pay the full hire. The company initiated arbitration in London earlier this year under the London Maritime Arbitrators Association after the unpaid balance reached about $28.2m in June. Hunter’s tanker exposure is centred on two scrubber-fitted VLCCs chartered in at fixed rates and chartered out on floating-rate arrangements linked to the Baltic Exchange TD3C benchmark. The dispute comes as the group prepares for a strategic transition with its existing VLCC charter arrangements approaching expiry. Hunter appointed Erik Mathiesen as permanent chief executive from October 1, tasking him with overseeing the company’s current operations and developing its next phase as the vessels are redelivered.

items.summary: Japan’s Tokyo Gas has acquired an Indonesian LNG infrastructure developer, paving the way for a new domestic shipping network supplying power stations across the country’s vast eastern archipelago. The Japanese utility, together with its wholly owned subsidiary Tokyo Gas Asia, has acquired 100% of PT AGP Indonesia Utama, which is developing a project to distribute domestically produced LNG using small-scale carriers and floating infrastructure. The venture will involve Indonesian state electricity company PLN’s fuel procurement arm, PLN Energi Primer Indonesia, and local shipping company PT Suasa Benua Sukses. The initial development envisages one floating LNG facility, six onshore installations and a small-scale LNG carrier serving six locations across Sulawesi and the Maluku Islands. The shipping network will operate around a central hub, with the LNG carrier supplying five other destinations. The acquisition gives Tokyo Gas a foothold in a market where geography presents both a challenge and an opportunity for small-scale gas shipping. Indonesia comprises more than 17,000 islands, many of which depend on relatively expensive diesel-fired power generation because of limited access to pipeline infrastructure. The proposed LNG distribution network is intended to reduce generation costs, cut emissions and lessen reliance on imported petroleum products.

items.title: German ports demand national funding pact
items.original_title: German ports demand national funding pact
items.summary: German port operators are pressing Berlin for a national funding partnership, arguing that infrastructure essential to trade, energy security and industrial supply chains cannot remain a purely regional responsibility. The Allianz Deutsche Häfen renewed its call at a Berlin gathering this week, bringing together port executives, industrial groups, retailers and federal transport representatives. Participants included parliamentary transport state secretary Christian Hirte and Lidl Germany boss Friedrich Fuchs. Salzgitter chief executive Gunnar Groebler argued that ports deserve the same national recognition as energy networks. “We should also treat our ports as what they are: strategic infrastructure of national interest,” he said. Participants stressed that spending must extend beyond terminals to the roads, railways and waterways connecting them with industry and consumers. The alliance’s wider demands include substantially higher federal contributions to port funding and money from Germany’s special infrastructure fund to tackle the modernisation backlog. Its members include bremenports, Brunsbüttel Ports, Duisburger Hafen, Hamburg Port Authority, Seehafen Kiel, Lübeck Port Authority, Niedersachsen Ports and Rostock Port. The group wants faster delivery and closer coordination between government, industry and port operators, presenting reliable gateways as a prerequisite for German competitiveness rather than a concern confined to coastal states.

items.title: Old LNG carriers keep changing hands
items.original_title: Old LNG carriers keep changing hands
items.summary: Sales of vintage large LNG carriers remain brisk as the secondhand market keeps ageing LNG tonnage afloat after the Strait of Hormuz conflict escalated in late February, with disruptions to regional LNG exports adding uncertainty to global supply. The latest sale has been completed by South Korean shipowner and manager Kmarin Group, selling the 18-year-old, 152,000 cu m Kmarin Diamond to Indonesian buyers for around $65m. Indonesian players have been among the most active buyers of ageing gas carriers this year. The first is the 18-year-old, steam-powered LNG carrier Tangguh Batur (145,700 cu m), reportedly sold for $30m. NYK has also sold the 2013-built, 177,427 cbm Grace Dahlia to Golar LNG for conversion. In August, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (K Line) sold its 20-year-old Arctic Voyager (142,759 cu m) for $28.5m to Karpowership interests, with the steam-powered vessel earmarked for conversion into a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU). This week on the recycling side, BW has let go of the 2007-built LNG carrier Kano, a vessel reported to have cracked cargo tanks. The ship has been sold for recycling in India at $530 per ldt. LNG Kano is the seventh LNG carrier to be sent for recycling this year.

items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd exits MSC and ONE Asia–South America pact
items.summary: Mediterranean Shipping Co (MSC) and Ocean Network Express are restructuring their vessel-sharing partnership between Asia and South America’s east coast, with Hapag-Lloyd dropping out of the existing three-carrier arrangement. MSC said that the current agreement covering the Ipanema service would end in its present form, leaving the Swiss carrier and Singapore-based ONE to operate the weekly service jointly. The first sailing under the revised agreement is scheduled to depart Shanghai on April 3, 2027. MSC will contribute additional ships to replace capacity associated with Hapag-Lloyd’s departure. ONE confirmed that it would continue operating the trade under its East Coast South America Express 1, or SX1, brand, maintaining weekly sailings between major Asian export centres and South America’s principal container gateways. The revised service will connect Shanghai, Ningbo, Shekou, Hong Kong and Singapore with Brazilian ports including Santos, Paranaguá, Navegantes and Rio Grande, as well as Montevideo and Buenos Aires.ONE said the final rotation remains subject to further operational review. The move ends a longstanding three-way cooperation on the route. MSC, ONE and Hapag-Lloyd expanded their Asia–South America east coast partnership in late 2018, with ONE adding weekly services to broaden coverage between the two regions. The latest restructuring leaves MSC and ONE continuing their cooperation while Hapag-Lloyd withdraws from the vessel-sharing arrangement.

Long established as cargo-handling facilities, they are becoming multi-functional nodes at the intersection of the energy transition, digitalisation and infrastructure resilience: gateways for conventional trade, industrial platforms for renewable energy and sustainable fuels, receiving terminals for hydrogen, ammonia and captured CO2, and marshalling hubs for offshore wind. The transformation is not voluntary. Whether a global fuel intensity standard and carbon pricing mechanism is adopted, and in what form, determines whether the EU’s regional measures remain the operative constraint on shipping calling at European ports or become one layer of a two-tier system. Brent moved from below $60 at the start of 2026 to above $100, European gas prices rose by between 40% and 67%, and the Commission’s spring 2026 forecast revised its Brent assumption upwards by 46%. items.summary: LR2 product tankers loaded on average 2.1 million barrels per day (mbpd) of clean products during the first three quarters of 2026, 0.8 mbpd less than in the same period of 2025. In 2025, more than 40% of clean product volumes carried by LR2s were loaded in the Persian Gulf, equivalent to 1.2 mbpd. Following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, this fell to 0.4 mbpd in 2026, accounting for just 18% of all clean product volumes loaded on LR2s. However, the decline in clean products has been more than offset by increased crude oil and heavy product volumes carried by LR2s. Despite the increase in volumes, total tonne-mile demand rose by only 2% year-on-year in the same period. Higher volumes from the Mediterranean and the Americas accounted for 80% of the increase in crude oil and heavy product volumes, although LR2s gained volumes in almost all loading regions. In the US and Canada, the increase in crude oil and heavy product volumes loaded on LR2s exceeded the overall increase in exports from both countries. items.original_title: Dry Bulk Shipping Fleet Growing, But Ageing as Well

The main feature of this expansion is not simply its pace, but its uneven distribution. Handysize capacity has grown much faster than the rest of the fleet since end-2023, while Capesize/Newcastlemax supply has expanded considerably more slowly. The dry bulk orderbook has increased from around 8.0% of the fleet in DWT terms at the end of 2023 to approximately 15.0% currently. Around 12.8% of the existing dry bulk fleet by vessel count is already more than 20 years old, with the proportion even higher in several smaller and mid-sized segments. Total seaborne dry bulk trade is expected to increase by around 1.7% in 2027, with iron ore growing at a similar pace, while coal and grains remain comparatively subdued. Bauxite continues to stand out as the strongest growth area, with volumes expected to rise by around 7.3%, while minor bulks are also projected to post moderate gains. At the same time, the ageing fleet and the possibility of stronger demolition mean that the headline orderbook may overstate the true increase in effective capacity.

It brought together traders, producers, consumers, brokers, analysts, investors and risk managers to discuss the forces reshaping global commodity markets. items.original_title: Supertankers Racing to Middle East Worsen Global Ship Crunch
items.summary: Supertankers are racing to the Middle East to cash in on soaring fees for carrying oil through the Strait of Hormuz , exacerbating a global shortage of vessels that has spiked freight rates. Crude flows through the waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf to international markets, have recovered to near pre-war levels in recent weeks despite continued attacks on ships. But the perils of the trade have prompted tanker fees to skyrocket: Moving oil from the gulf to East Asia costs more than six times as much as it did prior to the conflict. Meanwhile, crude producers outside of the Middle East — particularly in the Americas – are still maintaining high levels of output, even as flows from the Persian Gulf rebound. At least one VLCC was offered this week to sail from the US Gulf to Japan at a potential record fee of $82 million, or more than $40 a barrel. For the Persian Gulf to East Asia journey, which takes about three weeks, assessed supertanker rates reached an all-time high of nearly $1.4 million per day on Wednesday. The scarcity and sky-high fees for supertankers have prompted a switch to smaller Suezmax and Aframax vessels for non-Middle Eastern routes.

The 2026 Supply Chain Planning Benchmark Report , based on data from over 2,500 Netstock customers and a survey of more than 150 users at businesses with less than $250m in annual revenue, shows shippers under unceasing strain managing their supply chains. For one thing, the percentage of SMBs sourcing from two or more regions grew, from 45% in 2024 to 55% in 2026. This points to a fundamental shift in the challenges with which supply chain planners are struggling. The report said that, last year, supply chain planning was largely dictated by trade policies – tariffs – which brought about an emphasis on front-loading and building buffer stock. Emerging Chinese carrier CULines is said to have firm plans for an Asia-Middle East service, beginning in late 2026 or early 2027.
